public_title: Why Kids Laugh at Story Twists 🧠
hook: You squint when a story ends unexpectedly.

sections.title: Story
sections.narration: You squint when a story ends unexpectedly. Ancient humans actually laughed at sudden shifts in fate. In the 1970s, psychologists studied these reactions and found strong signals. The result? Your brain enjoys breaking predictions. When a twist happens, it releases dopamine. That is a reward chemical. Kids show this clearly. They react to surprise endings more than adults do. Why? Their brains are still learning patterns. A twist proves they were wrong. That feeling is good. It means their mind worked hard. Then it got a treat. That's it. It is not just noise. It is a victory. Researchers call this prediction error. It tells you when to listen. So why do we think kids just want simple plots? Because we forget how learning works. Learning requires being surprised. The viewer's doubt is natural. But the fact remains. Surprise fuels growth. So next time you watch a kid react, remember. You squint when a story ends unexpectedly.

claims.claim: Sudden unexpected events trigger a dopamine release as a reward signal when predictions are broken.
Children exhibit stronger reactions to unpredictable story outcomes than adults, indicating active pattern learning.

theme: Kids React to Surprising Story Endings
